title: Letting in the Darkness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating an authentic and honest relationship with oneself through the guidance of a trusted teacher or "friend." This process involves acknowledging and working with one's own darkness, imperfections, and fears in order to grow and transform. By embracing this inner work, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and connect more deeply with others, ultimately finding greater freedom from suffering and cultivating a more authentic spiritual practice.
topics: Buddhist teachings on imperfection and darkness

sentences.text: So as we were sitting our long retreat this last week, leading up to our woman's ancestor's ceremony, which we did on Friday, one of our senior woman teachers in the lineage family fell at her home in California and went into a coma.
She spent the last several days of our sesshin time, our retreat time, lying unconscious, surrounded by friends and students.
Then she passed away on Sunday morning, the day after the end of our Samish sesshin.
This zazen teacher in California, her name was Sobon Catherine Tanis.
I think she was in her middle or late 80s.
She started Zen practice with Suzuki Roshi sometime in the early 1960s, I think.
At the time she was in her late 30s and most of the other students were like 20 or 19, so she was an old person at the time, from their point of view.
Catherine Tanis was one of the sort of core, there was a group of maybe, I don't know how many, a lot.
It's amazing that the San Francisco Zen Center just started at a certain moment in time when people were just able to give their lives over to it for decades.
So Catherine was one of those people who lived in residence for some decades.
I met her in 1987 when we were sitting a sesshin in the large basement zendo at San Francisco Zen Center's city center building, big building, they own a whole block.
They converted the basement to a zendo, big enough for about a hundred people, I think it was full.
I think it was the first seven day sesshin I ever sat, and she was right across from me.
I don't know if I ever exchanged any words with her, but I was really impressed with her, just her bearing and the way she was.
And I learned a really useful thing about the formal oryoki meal form, which I learned from Catherine by watching her.
You get something stuck between your teeth in oryoki, which is a very formal, polite, Japanese thing.
It's polite to cover your mouth and stick your finger in your mouth.
I always remember that it's useful sometimes.

So it's strange for me, because I don't really know her, and there's quite a large number of people from the American Zen movement, especially San Francisco Zen Center, whom I have just memories like that of.
I don't know if I ever talked to her in person.
I just felt a lot of connection.
As a 21 year old, 22 year old student in that time, I was just a sponge for all this.
I wasn't even sure if I was interested in the long term in Zen practice, just trying it on is how I felt.

But somehow I had these impressions and these memories of people that I hold inside me, from what was happening from my point of view 25 years ago in this interesting little society of Zen practice in California.
And then each of us has that.
Each of us has within us these histories and these impressions, these connections with other human beings and other plants and animals and places that somehow we keep warm in our heart.
We're each of us a kind of time capsule.
It's hard to remember that each person we meet is a different time capsule, a completely different set of this, whatever it is.
And it's more than just memories, isn't it?
It's more than just thoughts.
It's something warmer and more connected than that.
That's how I feel about Catherine Tanis, even though I don't know if I saw her again at Green Gulch or at Tassajara.
I don't remember, but I remember her at sesshin getting the stuff out from between her teeth with her finger.
It makes me think also of other people in [unclear: "the song and piece of We Meet"].
I was talking to Dorothy Hoskins about a month ago.
She was a member here.
She's 78 or 79.
She was telling me how much she loves to see the flowers on the altar here.
Has she told you the story?

The reason she loves to see the flowers on the altar is that when she was growing up on a farm in Oklahoma in the 1930s, they were too poor to really be able to afford land or money for seed and water and fertilizer for flowers.
So they didn't really have flowers.
They had a small kitchen garden, and then the crops started very close to the edge of the house and went off into the distance as far as you can see.
That was still barely enough to support their family in those days.
So she has that time capsule in her, and the flowers bring that to mind for her all these years later, 70 years later.
Every one of us sitting here, or anybody who listens to this at home, if the batteries hold out, each of us is a kind of trustee, a trustee of reality.
Not that we cling to our memories or think that our memories are better than someone else's memories, but there's a richness there that we can't deny that comes forward into our life all the time.
Sometimes when something dramatic happens, or we have something in the past that was dramatic, it comes forward really strongly, like when somebody dies.
Then we bring something to that turning, to that moment.

Another connection I had with Catherine Tanis is that she ended up being the abbot, or abbess, I'm not sure which term she used, of the Santa Cruz California Zen Center a couple of years after I left Santa Cruz, because I went to college there.
So I never met her there either.
I was sitting at the Santa Cruz Zen Center, I think starting about 1985 or 86.
I'd stopped there on my bike and joined the morning practice.
I think of it as our Saturday morning practice.
There were like three people there.
And yet it was somehow very important to me.
I didn't really understand it.
I didn't really talk to them about it.
I remember one time they invited me to tea, and I just felt it was too overwhelming.
I never went inside the house.
I only went into the zendo.
I would sit with them, chant the Heart Sutra, and get back on my bike and ride up to the university.
But a little bit later, Catherine Tanis was the abbot, and earlier at that same center, Kobun Chino was a teacher there, Edie's first teacher.
So there are these webs.
And right now our dear friend and Sangha member, Chris Burkhart, is practicing at Santa Cruz Zen Center.
She's spending a year in Santa Cruz working, for some complicated, clever retirement reasons of her own.

She didn't really even expect to be sitting regularly at the Santa Cruz Zen Center, but it turns out because of where she's living and her schedule and how intense it is, she's sitting more there than she ever sat here.
She goes there every day.
She lives downtown, and it's close, and they have more of a daily schedule there, and teachers in residence, so it's easier for them to maintain a daily schedule.
So she's there a lot.
And she was part of the group that was sitting at Catherine's bedside while we were in sesshin.
She was sitting with Catherine, with the teachers and members and friends.
I'm sure not a lot, she was working, but she was there at least a few times.
And I think she was around there on the morning when she died, on Sunday morning, though I'm not sure about the exact moment.
So we have so many connections.
There are so many ways that our lives touch each other across time and across space.
Each life impossible to really hold or symbolize completely.
And there are billions of these lives, right?
Billions.
Each one so rich, so full.
So here's a poem.
Now, I mentioned before that the great benefit of Dharma transmission turns out to be you get on very exclusive email lists.
So I'm on exclusive Zen teacher email lists now.
So I see the inner workings of the American Zen establishment, at least the ones that choose to write email.
Squabbles and beautiful things and everything.
There were some really bad squabbles a month ago.
Lately it's been very beautiful.
There were many appreciations on the email of Catherine, and people talking about times they'd practiced with her.
One woman sent this poem by Jane Hirschfield in memory of Catherine, and I want to share this poem with you.
It's called "Rebus."
And then there's a note.
I'll tell you the note first.
The note at the end says a rebus is a representation of words in the form of pictures or symbols, often presented as a puzzle.
So it's words representing pictures representing words.
Here's the poem "Rebus" by Jane Hirschfield.
*You work with what you are given, the red clay of grief, the black clay of stubbornness going on after, clay that tastes of care or carelessness, clay that smells of the bottoms of rivers or dust.
Each thought is a life you have lived or failed to live.
Each word is a dish you have eaten or left on the table.
There are honeys so bitter no one would willingly choose to take them.
The clay takes them, honey of weariness, honey of vanity, honey of cruelty, fear.
This Rebus, slip and stubbornness, bottom of river, my own consumed life.
When will I learn to read it?
Painfully, slowly, uncolored by hope or desire, not to understand it but only to see.
As water given sugar sweetens, given salt grows salty, we become our choices.
And yes, each no, sorry, we become our choices.
Each yes, each no continues.
This one a ladder, that one an anvil or cup.
The ladder leans into the darkness, the anvil leans into the silence.*
*The cup sits empty.
How can I enter this question the clay has asked?
This Rebus, the red clay of grief, the black clay of stubbornness going on after.
Clay that tastes of care or carelessness, clay that smells of the bottoms of rivers or dust.
Each thought is a life you have lived or failed to live.
Each word is a dish you have eaten or left on the table.
There are honeys so bitter no one would willingly choose to take them.
The clay takes them.*
*Honey of weariness, honey of vanity, honey of cruelty, fear.
This Rebus, slip and stubbornness, bottom of river, my own consumed life.
When will I learn to read it?
Painfully, slowly, uncolored by hope or desire.
Not to understand it but only to see.
As water given sugar sweetens, given salt grows salty.
We become our choices.
Each yes, each no continues.
This one a ladder, that one an anvil or cup.
The ladder leans into the darkness, the anvil leans into its silence.
The cup sits empty.
How can I answer this question the clay has asked?*
So that's Jane Hirschfield.
I'll put it on the internet.
The choice of this poem to honor Catherine Tanis, who had just died, is extra touching if you know who sent it.
I think it's okay to say who sent it.
It was sent by a woman named Shinge Roko Sherat.
Shinge Roshi is the new abbot of the Zen Studies Society in Japan, which is one of our American Zen sanghas that has been really rocked and torn apart by sexual misconduct.
So she knows what she's talking about, about all that.
Yes, no, sweet, salty.
Her teacher, whom I think she really loves very much and probably doesn't know what to think about, has been a serial sexual predator for decades, it turns out.
Edo Shimano is his name.
And at the very same time [unclear: "a skillful and understand their life and understand the way he was in practice"] and has many very upright, very moral disciples.
So it's very strange.
So who knows what Edo Shimano has in him.
It has caused him [unclear: "molest and confused"] and we don't think quite rape but close, very close, and abusing his spiritual and charismatic power to convince women to have sex with him.
So I don't know what Catherine Tanis thought about that, or if she and Shinge ever talked about it, but I was really struck by her choice of that poem and what she's working on.
Because we have so much darkness in us too.
So our practice has to be a celebration of the whole thing, right?
Or else it's not real, it's not honest.
And sometimes during our intensive retreats like the one we just had, we become [unclear: "in us"].
Each other person is mirroring our light and our darkness.
Norman actually spoke about the physics of light.
I'm not sure if his physics was always quite perfect, but it was cool though.
It made good spiritual points: that we have inside all of us the honey that's so bitter that no one would take it.
We have within us the weariness, the vanity, carelessness.
Late in sesshin and I said something hurtful to somebody, and it was really painful to see that darkness coming out of my lips.
We worked it out and apologized, and I think both of us knew that what we say is in a way completely our responsibility, right?
We said it.
In a way it's emerging from a complex web of causes and conditions in us that we barely understand.
So the darkness is there and we work with it.
We notice it when it arises.
We take responsibility.
Bringing forth this darkness allows us to stop hiding, recognize in our sense of separation from others that we are kind of caught in a double bind all the time, a little bit.
On the one hand we really want to be seen, right?
We want to be recognized, made whole through the mirror of the seeing of others.
We want to be seen as a full person, worthy and awake.
But at the same time we want to hide the wicked thoughts, the meanness, the cruelty, the depression, the addiction that is also in us.

So somehow our process is unfolding and being a mirror for each other in our sangha life, and our practice has to find ways to include and allow for the light and the darkness, and to allow people to express both sides with full support from us.
We need to be careful about how we respond.
Sometimes it's just giving people space to express the dark side of their life.
It's not necessarily a cry for help or something we have to fix or repair.
It could be just letting it out, letting it breathe.
So here's a talk Catherine Tannis herself gave in 2003.
In the beginning of her little talk she quotes the same poet, Jane Hirschfield.
Here's what Catherine Tannis says about this being hidden and mirroring.
She's not exactly making the same point I'm trying to make, but it's close, and it's interesting.
I only know of a few talks of hers that are published online.
Some priests are constantly writing books and recording themselves and spreading their juju all over the internet.
I'm afraid I seem to be one of those.
Her teacher Norman is too.
But many other priests are not so much.
Talks aren't recorded.
It's just really about the situation, being where they are.
Once in a while they write a short talk for the newsletter, and maybe that gets published or somebody types it up.
So this is one of those talks, a short talk in a newsletter sometime.
Catherine wrote:
*In a recent essay the poet Jane Hirschfield writes, at Ryonji in Kyoto there's a famous rock garden.
In the way it's designed, wherever in it a person stands, one of the fifteen rocks cannot be seen.
The garden reminds that always something unknowable is present, just beyond what can be perceived or comprehended.
And that something, the thing that's hidden, is as much part of the real as any other stone amid the raked gravel.*
You know, this is a very famous rock garden.
I'll read that again.
*At Ryonji in Kyoto there's a famous rock garden.
Wherever in it a person stands, one of the fifteen rocks cannot be seen.
The garden reminds that always something unknowable is present, just beyond what can be perceived or comprehended.
And that something is as much part of the real as any other stone amid the raked gravel.*
Catherine goes on:

*Her beautiful essay reminds me of what one reviewer said about the late poet Philip Whelan, who was also a Zen priest, that he was not the best known of the Beat poets, but his experiments and his writing allowed them to write the work that they wrote.
You might say that Philip's contribution is hidden in the work of others, because we live in the lives of others, sometimes acknowledged, sometimes not.
These unrecognized connections among us are included in what we call our interdependent existence.
In our last newsletter we quoted Kobun Chino Roshi saying, "How to know your true self is something we cannot do alone.
We have to do it with someone who is able to accept our vow."*
*How to know your true self is something we cannot do alone.
We have to do it with someone who is able to accept our vow.* Catherine goes on:
*We have to practice with someone who is big enough to perceive our deepest self, our deepest intention, and turn us to it again and again.
Our true nature, our true self, is hidden in our consciousness, hidden from ourselves.
A true teacher like Koben Roshi or Suzuki Roshi sees our true nature.
In seeing and speaking to it, they allow us to also believe in it, to believe in our openness, receptivity, generosity, non-resistance, and loving kindness.
Help us to see those things in ourself.*
*What is known and not known by us about our inner motivations and intentions is the investigation of practice.
We know on one level, and we don't know on another level.
In her essay, Jane quotes Michael Dickinson on our contradictions, that we are most comfortable being hidden, yet yearn to be seen.
We are most comfortable being hidden, yet we yearn to be seen.
I would add we are quite fearful to see our inner mind.
We fear what demons might lurk, and the gift of practice is to allow us to gradually be drawn into this realm of the unknown and accompanied by a trustworthy friend who can help us to enter there.*
And that's really experientially true in our practice, and you see it maybe more clearly in an intensive retreat.
It's not like you choose to go there.
You're just drawn there.
Catherine goes on:
*In Christianity, the self measures or experiences itself by its receptivity to God or the universe.
In Buddhism, there is no permanent identifiable self.
The reality we call self, which seems to do the work of liberation, is a changing continuum, changing on every breath.

Within the self, there does seem to be an unchanging self, maybe like the observer of all this, which journeys through these changes and knows itself only as endless transformation, not hidden, but also seen.*
She goes on a bit longer, but I'll just leave that for you to read later on the web, just for time.
Along that same theme, you have the self that's sort of caught, right, in the story, in the drama, and that sense that there's something deeper, something going on a journey with that self.
Not some other self that can fix that self, but a self that understands itself as a non-self, understands itself as transformation, as each moment, transformations of consciousness.
And so are we just a collection of light and darkness, what's hidden and what's seen?
Or are we the observer of light and darkness, this unchanging self that Catherine Tanis mentions?

And of course the Buddha would remind us to not worry too much about these questions of what we actually are, only so much as it helps us to understand how to connect, how to suffer less, how to help others.
We make choices.
We say yes, we say no.
Experience unfolds the way it needs to.
Suffering and confusion increases sometimes.
Awakening and clarity increases sometimes.
So just to remind ourselves that we are a process.
We process and we process, or we process and process.
Processing in a procession together, and living the process of our inner work together in this procession.
That's another talk, still in the envelope.
I'm going to share a song with you, because sometimes all this is expressed through the arts.
In a way you could think about Zen practice itself as an art form, not so much a technique to get something, and ritual as an art form.
It's like a performance art piece, mixed together.
So I'm going to try to further this up.
One of the things we learned in Japan, when we went there summer before last, is that there is a contemporary Soto Zen movement called Baika.
I probably mentioned this before in the slideshow about Japan.
Baika is a singing practice.
When we think of Zen, it's sort of monotone.
This is a melodic singing practice, which was developed in the 1950s in Japan based on another lineage of Buddhism, the Tendai and Shingon lineages.

Apparently it's been very popular, and it's led to a bit of a revival of Soto Zen in Japan, because it's the kind of thing that groups of people, it might be mostly groups of women, I'm not sure, can get together and really do as a community practice.
For whatever reason, Baika, maybe because it's more intensely situated inside the Japanese culture, didn't make the leap to America the way Zazen did, the way the meditation did.
So we're in Japan.
Shingo-san and his wife, Shichitsuse-san, showed us a few Baika songs, and they sang one with us.
I think it was simple enough that we might be able to learn it.
So what I brought on the laptop, if I can fire it up, is a video with the audio of him singing it to us.
And then I asked Karen Fitzgerald to transcribe a notation.
They invented this bizarre notation for Baika, which she tried to explain to us, but it made no sense to us whatsoever.
And the other thing that's great about Baika, it's not just like you sit down and sing the songs.
This is Japan.
You'll see some of this, I hope, on the video.
It's small.
There's a whole ritual before you even begin to sing, and there's this little kit.
In addition to singing the songs, they have two different kinds of little bells that they ring.
And the little bells are carefully placed in a certain kind of cloth, which is wrapped in a certain way.
And what he told us is, for the first six months of your Baika training, you're not allowed to sing or play the instruments.
You attend the meeting, and you learn how to get the instruments out.
So, yeah, Americans would never do that, right?
Like, ah, come on, can I sing this?
So, yeah, this needs to befriend our trusted friend, exactly knowing who they are, so it's a faith practice in some ways, trusting that there is a trusted friend.
Right.
I just think it's so easy for us to maybe project onto our teachers, make them our trusted friend.
Well, she's saying that what the teacher does is just help you have faith in your own experience, right?
In your own self.
So it might be that the spiritual teacher can role play the trusted friend for you as a way to help you meet that person inside yourself, or outside yourself.
Maybe the trusted friend is a bird flying in the sky.
So we passed this out.
She didn't type it up, so hopefully we can read Karen's handwriting okay.
My vision here is that I'll still be around.
I'll be in Bellingham mostly all summer, and I'm going to take a little bit of a sabbatical from Wednesday night, so I'm leaving you with the song.
We'll listen to him and I'll try to explain the words, and then we'll probably sing it separately from him because he sings in a really awkward key.
And she and Karen transcribed it to, I guess, just C major.
There's no flats or sharps.
Yeah, I think he's singing in A minor or something like that.
A minor seventh or something.
So let me see if I can bring this up.
And now the other thing to do is scoot in really close.
Scoot in here.
We'll have a listen.
Scoot around the campfire here.
And we're going to watch something here.
It's okay if you can't see.
I thought of doing a projection, but I thought no.
So this is the grandson of the person we call Suzuki Roshi, the grandson of Shunryu Suzuki, whom we never met, and the son of Uitsu Suzuki.
I mean, the local scene is Suzuki Roshi, right?
Yeah.
I wonder how many generations of priests are there?
Yeah, I don't know.
Certainly it's Suzuki Roshi's father.
Yeah.
It's five.
And he's inside, we're inside Rinsoin temple, outside Yaizu, Japan.
And now we're on the train south of the temple.
It's really hard to remember when it was founded.
This temple was founded in 1492.
Something good happened in 1492.
That's good.
So it's been there for 500 years.
So what this song is, it's Namu.
Can you read it?
Namu Honshi.
So Namu means honor.
Honshi is teacher.
So honoring the teacher.
Shaka is Shakyamuni, like Buddha.
And Nyorai is Buddha.
So that means our regular Buddha.
Shaka Nyorai is Buddha.
So it's basically just homage to the teacher.
Shats repeated what they're doing.
Maybe I have his wife too.
We were quite blown away by all this, as you can imagine.
And so this is the simplest song.
There's this enormous songbook with much more elaborate songs.
But this is one that he...
On the Sunday program, which was the community program, the women would do this kind of singing, and it was very elaborate.
It was very strange.
Late 30s maybe.
He was at the temple.
That's his job.
People coming and going all day.
He would run into town to...
This is Kate playing Shaka Hachi and me just wandering around the temple grounds.
No, no, Kate was on the canvas.
Sadly, Kate wasn't there.
Go up a little bit.
So let's just try it and see what happens.
This is a simple one.
Anything you can do.
You can come with a little keyboard and just keep the song in tune.
I think we could learn this.
We could practice it.
Isn't it beautiful?
It's devotional music.
It sounds Jewish.
Does it sound a little Jewish?
Yeah.
Yeah, prayer.
It's like singing a prayer.
It does look Hebrew, for Hebrew prayer.
That makes you want to start.
That's nice.
It's very military.
So you don't have his wife?
I might.
I might have it at home.
I kind of brought the wrong...
It's lovely.
Thank you.
We can figure out a way to work on it little by little.
It would just be a wonderful thing just to have in our song a vocabulary to be able to sing this song.
I don't know if we'd ever go further in this in the genre.
